h1: Planning whisky flights for a dinner
title: Planning Whisky Flights for a Dinner | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan whisky flights for a dinner: pour sizes, the order of whiskies, pairing with courses and keeping the evening responsible.
teaser: Whisky at dinner works when the flight is planned like the menu. Here is how to do it.
standfirst: Pairing whisky with a meal takes more planning than opening a bottle after dessert. Pour sizes, order and food all need thought. Here is a practical way to plan whisky flights for a dinner at home.
sections: Plan the flight around the menu

Start with the food, not the bottles. Write down each course and its strongest flavour: spice, smoke, sweetness, richness or acidity. Then choose a whisky that either matches that flavour or cuts through it.

Three whiskies across a meal is plenty: one with a starter or appetiser, one with the main course and one with dessert or after. Four is the upper limit. Any more and the later whiskies get lost.

Our guide to whisky and Indian food pairing covers specific dishes in detail.

At a dinner, whisky should be tasted, not drunk by the glass. A pour of 15 to 20 ml per whisky is enough to nose, taste and pair. Three such pours add up to 45 to 60 ml across the whole evening, which keeps the meal about food and conversation.

Put water on the table from the start, both for drinking and for adding to whisky. Highballs with plenty of soda work well with spicy starters and keep the strength down. Our guide to the whisky highball for Indian summers explains how to make a good one.

Use tulip shaped glasses for neat pours, one per whisky per guest if you can. If you do not have enough, rinse with water between whiskies. For highballs, use tall glasses with plenty of ice.

In a warm Indian dining room, keep the whisky bottles out of direct sun and pour just before each course. Do not chill the neat pours, because cold mutes aroma. Our guide to whisky glassware covers the options.

As with any tasting, go from light to heavy. A typical order:

  1. Starter: a light, fresh whisky, such as a Lowland or a light Speyside malt, or a highball. These suit lighter dishes such as tandoori fish, paneer tikka or salads.
  2. Main course: a richer whisky, such as a sherry cask malt or a bourbon. These stand up to rich gravies, roast meats or a mutton curry.
  3. Dessert or after: a peated malt, a PX cask whisky or an older, richer whisky. Smoke pairs surprisingly well with dark chocolate. Sweet sherry casks suit fruit-based desserts.

Peat goes last because smoke lingers. Serving it early would flatten every whisky that follows.

Two approaches help:

  • Match: pair similar flavours. Vanilla rich bourbon with a caramel dessert. Smoky malt with smoked or grilled meat.
  • Contrast: use the whisky to cut through. A crisp, light whisky against fried or fatty food. Water and soda against chilli heat.

High chilli heat and neat high strength whisky do not get on. The alcohol amplifies the burn of the chilli. For spicy courses, lower the strength with water or use a highball. For a fiery dish such as a Chettinad chicken or a laal maas, a long, cold highball is usually kinder than a neat pour.

Not every guest drinks. Some will drink less than others. Plan a non-alcoholic pairing for each course too, such as a ginger and lime cooler, a spiced buttermilk or good sparkling water. Offer every whisky as optional.

Make sure everyone has a safe way home. Arrange cabs, a driver or somewhere to stay. Never let anyone drink and drive. Keep food on the table for the whole evening.

Here is one way a three flight Indian dinner could run, as a starting point rather than a rule:

  • Starter: grilled prawns or paneer tikka with a light, grassy malt as a highball, about 30 ml whisky topped with chilled soda.
  • Main: a slow cooked mutton curry or a biryani with 20 ml of a sherry cask malt, neat with water on the side.
  • After: dark chocolate or a piece of fruit cake with 15 ml of a lightly peated malt.

Swap freely. If your guests prefer softer flavours, drop the peat and finish with a bourbon. The structure, light to heavy and small pours, matters more than the bottles.
A short card for each whisky

Guests enjoy a dinner flight more when they know what they are tasting. A small card for each whisky helps: name, region, age, cask and two or three aroma words to look for. It turns a drink into a guided experience and starts conversation.

Writing those cards well, with accurate aroma notes and a sensible pairing reason, is harder than it looks. It draws on exactly the nosing and tasting vocabulary that structured sensory training builds.

Your first step: pick one dish you cook well and one whisky you know. Taste them together at home before the dinner. Try the whisky neat, then with water, then as a highball. See which version suits the dish. One tested pairing is better than three guesses on the night.
faqs: How much whisky should I pour at a dinner?
Around 15 to 20 ml per whisky is enough to taste and pair, with three whiskies across the meal.
What order should whiskies be served at dinner?
Light to heavy: a fresh whisky with starters, a richer one with the main and peated or sweet sherry cask whisky last.
Does whisky go with spicy Indian food?
It can, but high strength makes chilli heat worse. Add water or serve a highball with spicy dishes.
How do I make a whisky dinner responsible?
Keep pours small, serve plenty of water and food, offer non-alcoholic pairings and make sure no one drives home.
